claims.text: In a randomised trial of 610 patients, 30-day readmission was 9.2 percent with remote monitoring and 12.8 percent with usual care (risk ratio 0.72, 95 percent CI 0.47 to 1.10).
claims.passage: Thirty-day readmission was 9.2 percent with remote monitoring and 12.8 percent with usual care (risk ratio 0.72, 95 percent CI 0.47 to 1.10).
claims.interpretation: A plausible benefit whose interval includes no effect; a larger real-world estimate is needed.

claims.text: A model-based analysis gave remote monitoring a 54 percent probability of being cost-effective at 50,000 per quality-adjusted life year, driven by an imprecise readmission effect.
claims.passage: remote monitoring had a 54 percent probability of being cost-effective at a threshold of 50,000 per quality-adjusted life year
claims.interpretation: A cost-effectiveness answer now would be a coin toss; the effect estimate is the missing input.

claims.text: Thirty-day readmission after cardiac surgery varied from 9 to 19 percent across 12 hospitals, and case mix explained about half of that variation.
claims.passage: Case mix, including age, frailty, ejection fraction, urgency and procedure type, explained about half of the variation between hospitals.
claims.interpretation: Centre comparisons must adjust for case mix and stable centre differences.

claims.text: With only two adopting and two comparison hospitals, conventional standard errors are far too small, and contamination of a comparison hospital should end its comparison period.
claims.passage: With only two adopting and two comparison hospitals, conventional standard errors are far too small
claims.interpretation: Use changes before and after adoption with honest few-cluster intervals and a contamination rule.

claims.text: Readmissions accounted for 58 percent of the mean 90-day post-discharge cost of 6,200 per patient.
claims.passage: Readmissions accounted for 58 percent of this cost
claims.interpretation: The cost case rests on readmissions avoided; a 90-day horizon captures most of it.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. One randomised trial and a systematic review suggest remote monitoring after cardiac surgery lowers readmission and emergency visits, but the cardiac estimates have intervals that include no effect. A model-based economic evaluation found cost-effectiveness to be close to a coin toss because it borrowed that imprecise effect. Readmission varies widely between hospitals, half of it explained by case mix, and methods work shows that comparisons of few adopting and non-adopting hospitals need before-and-after contrasts, honest few-cluster intervals and a rule for contamination. Readmissions drive most post-discharge cost. The missing input for the ministry is a fair real-world effect estimate with costs attached.
gradeRationale: Effect evidence imprecise and partly non-randomised; economic evidence rests on a single imprecise trial; methods guidance is strong but not an effect estimate.
summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; five claims, one with high uncertainty; certainty low.
